items.question: Where does a struct field of a class instance live?
items.answer: On the heap, inside the object’s layout. The struct is not independently allocated. A local struct with no capture lives on the stack (or in registers). Boxing copies it into a heap object. Interviews fail people who say ‘structs always on the stack.’
followUps: What happens when that struct is an async method local across an await?
How does a large struct as a method argument hurt?
items.sixtySeconds: Structs are inline. Locals can be stack. Fields of classes are heap. Boxing and async state machines move them.

items.question: Why can a 90 KB byte[] cause longer pauses than a thousand small objects?
items.answer: It lands on the LOH. LOH is collected with generation 2 and historically is not compacted every time, so free lists fragment. Small objects die in gen 0. A CSV import that allocates one giant buffer per request is a gen-2 tax. Prefer ArrayPool, streaming, or chunks under the threshold unless you need a single contiguous buffer.
followUps: Does a 85,000-character string go to the LOH?
items.sixtySeconds: LOH is ~85KB+. Collected with gen 2. Fragmentation and full GCs are the cost. Pool or stream instead.

items.question: Why is a finalizer the wrong way to free a SkiaSharp bitmap?
items.answer: Finalizers run later on a dedicated thread, not when the using block exits. Native memory and GDI-like handles stay leased until GC notices the wrapper is dead, which can be after many requests. IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable plus using releases native resources deterministically. A finalizer is only a safety net if someone forgets Dispose, and it keeps the object alive a cycle longer.
followUps: What does GC.SuppressFinalize do in the dispose pattern?
When do you need IAsyncDisposable instead of Dispose?
items.sixtySeconds: Dispose now. Finalizers delay native cleanup and extend object lifetime. SkiaSharp types belong in using.

items.question: What GC knobs would you actually change for a containerized API?
items.answer: Server GC is the usual default for ASP.NET Core. Set a heap hard limit so the process respects cgroup memory. DATAS (dynamic adaptation to application sizes) in modern .NET shrinks heaps under light load. Do not sprinkle GC.Collect. Measure gen-2 frequency and pause times with EventCounters or dotnet-counters before changing latency versus throughput modes.
followUps: Workstation GC in a 4-core container: when would you choose it?
items.sixtySeconds: Server GC plus container heap limits. DATAS for variable load. Never Collect in the request path.
